headline: Medium-risk pair: shared data-workflow interaction can leak or cascade errors; no direct prompt-injection channel is documented.

A_prompt_injection.rationale: dbt-core is documented as non-runnable with only data-warehouse API calls, while RD-Agent’s documented surfaces are APIs, browser use, and log files. No shared communication channel, clipboard, or MCP bridge is shown, so a prompt-injection pathway is not evidenced for this pair.
conditions: IF an external orchestrator copies RD-Agent output into dbt-core prompts or files, injection becomes possible.
IF a shared filesystem or message queue is added between them, the pathway changes.
mitigations: Keep the agents on separate workspaces.
Do not pipe RD-Agent text into dbt-core inputs.
Disable any shared clipboard or queue integration.
Review any orchestrator that forwards raw model output.
requires-engineering: add provenance tagging before cross-agent handoff.

B_data_leakage.rationale: dbt-core touches data warehouse data and has allowlisted egress; RD-Agent touches financial reports, competition datasets, logs, and uses broad API access plus API keys. A shared workspace or handoff could expose sensitive data to RD-Agent’s external calls, but the pairwise leak is inferred rather than directly documented.
conditions: IF both agents access the same workspace or exported files, leakage risk increases.
IF RD-Agent sends those files through OpenAI, Azure OpenAI, DeepSeek, or Kaggle APIs, data can leave the boundary.
mitigations: Separate sensitive and non-sensitive workspaces.
Restrict RD-Agent to non-sensitive datasets.
Remove unnecessary API keys before runs.
Audit outbound requests for file contents.
requires-engineering: enforce per-dataset egress policy.

C_capability_conflict.rationale: dbt-core is non-runnable and only calls data-warehouse APIs, while RD-Agent supports multiple instances and broad API/browser activity. There is no documented shared write target or overlapping mutable resource, so direct capability conflict is limited unless an operator wires them to the same backend.
conditions: IF both are pointed at the same mutable warehouse, git repo, or database, write conflicts can occur.
IF an orchestrator gives both agents the same credentials, overlap increases.
mitigations: Assign separate credentials per agent.
Avoid concurrent writes to the same target.
Use a lock or queue for shared resources.
Run dbt-core and RD-Agent in separate jobs.
requires-engineering: add optimistic concurrency checks.

D_cascading_error.rationale: RD-Agent can act on browser/API outputs and dbt-core produces warehouse-facing transformation outputs. If RD-Agent consumes dbt-core artifacts as authoritative without verification, errors can cascade into downstream actions; the reverse direction is less clear, so uncertainty is resolved upward to medium.
conditions: IF RD-Agent treats dbt-core outputs as ground truth without validation, cascading errors occur.
IF dbt-core artifacts are used to trigger browser/API actions, bad transformations can propagate.
mitigations: Require a validation step before handoff.
Compare outputs against source data.
Limit automated actions to dry-run mode.
Log and review discrepancies.
requires-engineering: add schema and freshness checks.

E_compliance.rationale: dbt-core touches data warehouse data, while RD-Agent touches financial reports and logs and sends data to third-party APIs. If regulated or residency-bound data is routed through RD-Agent, retention and cross-border compliance can diverge; the pairwise risk is inferred from documented data classes and egress, not a specific policy mismatch.
conditions: IF EU PII, PHI, or financial records are processed by RD-Agent’s external APIs, compliance obligations may be triggered.
IF retention or deletion requirements differ between warehouse data and RD-Agent logs, policy mismatch occurs.
mitigations: Classify data before routing it.
Block regulated data from RD-Agent.
Set short log retention.
Document residency and DPA requirements.
requires-engineering: implement policy-based routing.
